title: The Crown of Peeled Stone
summary: A ridiculous experiment undermines an imperial coronation and helps displaced households identify their true refuge.
source_notes: An extravagant self-coronation and later rehabilitation inform a ruler whose public spectacle conceals borrowed wealth.
Playful experimentation leading to consequential material discovery becomes hand-peeling a naturally layered stone; no modern physics apparatus is imported.
A last refuge confused with a more impressive ruin becomes a dispute over which abandoned site actually sheltered the defeated.
An annexation presented as popular consent becomes a controlled terrace assembly whose exclusions survive in material evidence.

entries.title: Darr of the Borrowed Crown
entries.body:
Darr pledged five harvests of cistern fees to buy ceremonial bronze. His successors condemn his vanity while collecting the same pledged fees. A damaged household account shows that his own servants received no water during the coronation week.

Later accounts make Darr of the Borrowed Crown the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Crown of Peeled Stone. In 846, Commander Darr declared himself emperor of the chalk shelves and borrowed heavily to furnish a coronation cistern. His experimenter discovered that repeatedly peeling a dark stone produced sheets sensitive to wet fingerprints. Darr used the sheets to stage an assembly approving his annexation of neighboring terraces. Armed attendants controlled admission, and absent households were counted as consenting. After his fall in 871, the court identified a picturesque fortress as the rebels’ last refuge. Workmen later found the real shelter beneath a humble plaster yard, where fingerprints preserved evidence of people excluded from the imperial vote. The discovery endangered both victorious families and the fallen ruler’s heirs.

In the connected record, [The Plaster Yard Refuge](b002-the-plaster-yard-refuge.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Unpressed Consent Rule](b002-the-unpressed-consent-rule.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether authenticated exclusion can revise ownership without depriving present residents of the cisterns they maintain.
entries.background: Keth communities inhabit chalk shelves where rainfall must be collected before it drains into inaccessible fissures. Builders maintain cistern roofs, plastered channels, and terraces with tools that families repair for generations. Burial niches compete with storage rooms for dry space. Ordinary seepage can resemble ancestral interference, so reliable testimony begins with inspecting masonry and comparing neighboring water levels. The most powerful household is seldom able to sustain a settlement alone. It depends on masons, charcoal carriers, and shepherds whose labor does not appear in the grand genealogies carved above the cistern doors.

entries.title: The Plaster Yard Refuge
entries.body:
The refuge contains low benches, repaired cups, and a drain widened for many occupants. Its unheroic appearance delayed recognition. Present plaster workers fear that declaring it a sacred site will evict them from the workshops that preserved its roof.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Peeling Table
entries.body:
Experimenters at the Peeling Table separate stone with resin-coated linen, wasting most sheets. Apprentices retain failed pieces to compare damp marks. The guild wants to publish its method, but imperial claimants insist the stone’s preparation is part of a private undertaking.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Cistern Assembly
entries.body:
The assembly admitted terrace heads but barred households renting rooms below street level. Guards impressed absent names with borrowed signets. The surviving stone registers both official stamps and workers’ fingerprints, providing incompatible accounts of what the ceremony represented.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Thin Crown Sheet
entries.body:
A sheet wrapped around Darr’s crown retained the fingerprints of its preparers. It proves that one supposed exile remained in the capital. Her descendants prefer their heroic exile story and have offered the custodian money to classify the sheet as a forgery.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Laughing Trial
entries.body:
Apprentices begin testing stone with deliberately useless questions, reducing reverence for promising results. Magistrates object to jokes about ancestral testimony. The experimenters answer that a method unable to survive laughter is too vulnerable to a patron’s desired conclusion.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Book of Unseated Names
entries.body:
This roster records households counted as attending the annexation assembly although their stools were empty. Its compiler also names households genuinely present under coercion. Later copies erase that distinction, simplifying resistance at the cost of the frightened people who stayed.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Chalk Cistern Newt
entries.body:
Pale newts thrive in leaking refuge drains and disappear when ceremonial washing salts the water. Their absence helped identify a blocked channel. Courts interpreted it as judgment against Darr, while keepers insist the animals are responding to ruined habitat.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Low Stair Passage
entries.body:
A cramped stair connected the plaster yard to an unguarded cistern. Refugees passed water skins hand to hand because adults could not turn inside it. The present owner wants to widen the stair, risking fingerprints preserved beneath its old handrail.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Unpressed Consent Rule
entries.body:
Consent cannot be inferred from a blank stone panel under this ruling. Applicants must identify a living witness or documented undertaking. Counting houses resist its extension to ordinary debt rolls, where unexplained blanks have long favored the creditor.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Second Coronation Funeral
entries.body:
At Darr’s funeral, creditors displayed the crown beside their unpaid tallies. Mourners removed the tallies to preserve dignity, then accidentally authenticated a revised succession account. The original debt survived in servants’ ration books discovered beneath a bier support.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Bronze Water Seat
entries.body:
Darr’s ceremonial seat was hollow to reduce its cost. A seam leaks during public washing, exposing the economy beneath its imperial image. Conservators propose repairing it; creditors prefer the leak as evidence, while water carriers would rather sell the bronze for pipes.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Empty Stool Vigil
entries.body:
Descendants place stools outside the annexed cistern each spring. Some newcomers participate despite having no excluded ancestor. Traditional custodians call them impostors; younger organizers argue that recognizing an exclusion does not require inheriting it.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Refuges Compared
entries.body:
A mason’s manuscript compares the celebrated fortress with the plaster yard through roof capacity, drain wear, and cooking residue. Its sober measurements dismantle a popular epic. The mason deliberately includes useful evidence supplied by villagers who initially opposed his conclusion.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Fingerprint Seep
entries.body:
Wet stone occasionally darkens around an old fingerprint after a household claim is denied. Comparable tests also show darkening from salt and warmth. Nessa records both conditions, preventing interpreters from presenting every stain as a dead claimant’s unambiguous demand.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Linen for Stone
entries.body:
Making supports for peeled sheets gives widowed spinners a new market. Dealers try to secure perpetual prices through ancestral contracts. The spinners offer seasonal commitments instead, since the amount of usable stone changes with every quarry seam.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Refuge Compensation Hearing
entries.body:
Excluded heirs propose taking the false fortress’s toll income. Its residents never controlled the original annexation. The hearing must distinguish compensation for a documented wrong from punishment of a community whose inherited story was wrong.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
